transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-06-05 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Tom Reyes (CTO, Stratus), Maria Gonzalez (Lead ML), Ethan Liu (SRE)

Summary (auto): quick walkthrough of Redwood Optimize features: batching knobs, prefix / KV cache tradeoffs, and cost modelling; discussion about encryption, SSO, and POC plan.

00:00 Alex Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, i'll kick off real quick, im alex from redwood, priya our se is here too, we wanted to run through some recommendations specifically on batching and the kv/prefix cache that tend to move the needle for payments workloads.
01:02 Tom Reyes: Cool, yeah we ran into some cost surprises last quarter when volume spiked, so curious what you have, we have pretty tight latency SLOs, 95p under 200ms for single-turn chat flows.
01:27 Priya Kapoor: Right, totally. we'll show a couple of concrete configs. first question for you though - what's your current stack? are you on hosted api, or self-hosted endpoints? and roughly what's the average request size?
01:45 Maria Gonzalez: We're on a managed endpoint with another vendor now, not self-hosted. average prompt is 210 tokens, responses about 120 tokens, and we do a lot of short single-turn auth checks plus some multi-turn support flows.
02:10 Alex Chen: Great, that helps. two quick levers we recommend: batching (smaller per-request batching to keep latency low but still improve throughput) and prefix/kvcache for repetitive auth/context prefixes which can dramatically reduce per-token compute.
03:00 Tom Reyes: When you say prefix cache, do you mean storing KV state from common prefixes so subsequent calls reuse the kv cache? how does that affect memory on the gpu?
03:25 Priya Kapoor: Yep exactly. prefix caching stores the key/value attention cache for repeated prefixes. hit rate depends on how much of the prompt is stable - auth headers, system prompts, product descriptors. memory impact is mostly proportional to unique prefix count and sequence length; we showed earlier that for payments flows with a stable 80-token prefix you can see 40-60% cost reduction if hit rates are high.
04:12 Maria Gonzalez: That sounds promising. how do you quantify savings? do you have a cost model we can plug our traffic into?
04:30 Alex Chen: Yes, we'll share a spreadsheet. high level: for each 1M tokens generated we model compute vs memory vs amortized GPU overhead. with prefix cache assumptions we simulate hit rate scenarios (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%) and show delta in GPU-seconds and $/1M tokens.
05:05 Ethan Liu: Any gotchas about consistency or staleness if the prefix changes often?
05:20 Priya Kapoor: Good point - cache invalidation is important. we recommend keys scoped per-customer and TTLs; also fallbacks to full decode when prefix doesn't match. for sensitive data you can choose to not cache or cache only non-sensitive parts. integration supports KMS encryption at rest for cache blobs.
06:10 Tom Reyes: On security, we need SOC2 type II, SSO/SAML, and our own KMS/HSM integration if we do private. does redwood support that?
06:28 Alex Chen: Yes we do SOC2 attestations, SSO via SAML/okta, and for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. we'll attach our security packet and the KMS integration guide in the follow-up.
07:00 Maria Gonzalez: Back to batching - our traffic is bursty; sometimes we have many small requests concurrently. how do you pick batch size without blowing past our 200ms 95p?
07:22 Priya Kapoor: You tune two things: max batch size and max wait time (batching window). for latency-sensitive flows we recommend small max batch sizes (4-8) and tight wait times (2-5ms) combined with dynamic routing to lower-latency pools. Redwood Optimize suggests a per-route profile with expected token-length distribution so you get automated recommendations.
08:05 Tom Reyes: Any examples on the tradeoff? like x% cost saved vs latency percentiles?
08:20 Alex Chen: In our model, if you accept a 10ms median increase you might save 15-20% on token cost at that load, but at higher batch sizes the tail can widen; that's why we pair batching with prefix cache so you reduce compute per request and need smaller batches. we'll include example curves in the spreadsheet.
10:00 Maria Gonzalez: Do you support quantized runtime? we use some float16 models in house.
10:12 Priya Kapoor: Redwood runtime supports 4-bit/8-bit quantized variants and kernel selection to favor quantized paths; that often compounds savings. Note some quality tradeoffs exist and we recommend A/B tests.
11:05 Ethan Liu: For the POC, what baseline metrics should we capture?
11:20 Priya Kapoor: Capture P95 latency, tail latency (99), tokens per request, requests per second, prefix cache hit rate, and cost per 1M tokens. Also sample outputs for quality checks. We'll provide a test plan template.
12:05 Tom Reyes: About dedicated vs hosted: we're leaning to dedicated because of data residency and audit requirements. any immediate differences for batching/cache?
12:25 Alex Chen: Dedicated gives more predictable throughput and isolation which helps with consistent batch sizes; private deployment gives you control over KMS and network SSO. On hosted you get faster setup and Redwood manages the infra. For caching, both modes support prefix caching; private just gives you total control of cache storage if needed.
14:00 Maria Gonzalez: Any latency numbers from other customers in finance? we've seen some slides but curious real examples.
14:18 Priya Kapoor: We can share anonymized benchmarks: for a payments customer with similar workload, enabling prefix cache plus tuned batching dropped average token compute by ~48% and p95 latency stayed within 200ms when batch windows were <=5ms. We'll include these anonymized results.
16:00 Alex Chen: Ok let's sketch the pilot: 2 week POC, Redwood runs baseline tests against your representative traffic (you provide sample CSV), we enable prefix cache in a staging route, and measure hit rate and cost delta. If results look good we propose a phased rollout.
16:28 Tom Reyes: Sounds reasonable. licensing and pricing - do you do reserved capacity for dedicated? We may need a committed tier for heavy usage.
16:45 Alex Chen: Yes, Dedicated offers reserved capacity with monthly/annual commits and lower unit costs. We'll include pricing tiers in the doc bundle.
18:00 Maria Gonzalez: Any limitations for long context windows? our support flow sometimes reaches 8k tokens.
18:15 Priya Kapoor: Runtime supports long context but KV cache benefits most on repeated prefixes. For truly long contexts we look at segmentation, retrieval augmentation, and partial cache strategies. We'll flag best practices in the guide.
20:00 Ethan Liu: Are there any infra requirements for prefix caching on private? do we need extra redis or storage?
20:18 Priya Kapoor: For Private you can either use Redwood-managed cache within the private control plane or integrate with a customer-provided object store/redis; we documented the options in the integration guide. For hosted, Redwood handles storage.
22:05 Tom Reyes: Ok last question, SLAs and failover - if a dedicated pool has issues what's the fallback?
22:20 Alex Chen: We support smart routing and multi-pool fallbacks; you can set policies to fall back to hosted model variants with slightly higher cost but better availability. We'll show canary/AB rollout flows.
24:00 Maria Gonzalez: Great. any immediate blockers from our side?
24:10 Tom Reyes: Just internal compliance review but otherwise we can proceed with the POC, assuming security docs look good.
24:30 Alex Chen: Perfect. recap and next steps: we'll send the cost model spreadsheet, security packet, and POC test plan; Priya will propose POC dates and run baseline tests once we get sample traffic.
24:55 Priya Kapoor: i'll follow up with calendar invites and the test plan template.
25:10 Alex Chen: thanks everyone.

Transcript notes: occasional ASR errors: "kv cache" sometimes transcribed as "k v cash" in earlier recordings; speaker overlap occasionally.
